title: Where Should a Primate Field Course in Uganda Be Based? Kibale, Budongo and Bwindi Compared
meta_title: Primate Field Course in Uganda, Station by Station
meta_description: Plan a primate field course in Uganda: Kibale, Budongo and Bwindi stations, student park fees, research clearance and group logistics.
excerpt: How to plan a primate field course in Uganda for university groups: which field station to use, student fees and permits, a two-week outline and group logistics.
content:
A primate field course in Uganda is usually built around a university field station in Kibale National Park, Budongo Forest or Bwindi, with two to four weeks of guided forest work, chimpanzee observation, lectures and student projects. Most groups of 12 to 30 students base themselves at one station, then add a short savannah and gorilla extension at the end.

Course leaders rarely struggle to find primates in Uganda. The hard part is the rest: which station takes a group your size, whether students need research clearance, how park fees work for foreign students, and how to move 25 people and their kit safely across the west of the country. This guide answers those questions for anyone running a primate field course or a university study tour or field course in East Africa, from first email to the drive back to Entebbe.

Quick Facts

  • Main bases: Makerere University Biological Field Station (Kibale), Budongo Conservation Field Station (near Masindi), Institute of Tropical Forest Conservation (Ruhija, Bwindi)
  • Typical group: 12-30 students plus 2-4 staff; the Kibale station can house and feed courses of up to 60
  • Ideal length: 2-4 weeks at a station, plus 3-5 days of savannah or gorilla extension
  • Kibale park entry: US$40 per day for foreign non-residents, with 50% off for foreign students on short field courses for up to 10 days (UWA tariff, checked November 2026)
  • Best months: June-August and December-February, Uganda's two drier spells
  • Drive from Entebbe: about six hours to Kibale via Fort Portal

What Does a Primate Field Course in Uganda Actually Involve?

A primate field course in Uganda combines daily forest work with lectures, data collection and a student project, all based at a research station inside or beside a protected forest. Students on a primate field course learn observation and sampling methods on habituated primates, then design and run a short study of their own before writing it up.

Kibale alone holds 13 primate species across 795 km² of mostly tropical forest, so a single station gives students chimpanzees, red colobus, black-and-white colobus, red-tailed monkeys and grey-cheeked mangabeys within walking distance. That density is why so many universities bring a primate field course back year after year. A typical day starts with a dawn walk on station trails, moves to group work or analysis through the heat of the afternoon, and ends with a seminar after dinner.

The learning goals of a primate field course usually fall into three areas. The first is behaviour and ecology: activity budgets, feeding, ranging and group composition. The second is forest ecology and restoration, since logged, regenerating and old-growth patches sit side by side. The third is the human side: crop raiding, park-people relations and how primate tourism pays for protection. A strong primate field course weaves all three together, so students see a chimpanzee community as part of a landscape rather than as an exhibit.

How it differs from a school educational tour

A school trip moves every day or two and keeps each activity short. A university primate field course does the opposite: it stays put, repeats the same trails, and asks students to produce data. If your group is younger or the aim is broad exposure, our guide to a Uganda educational tour for schools covers that style of trip instead.

Which Field Station Should Host Your Course?

The right field station depends on your group size, your teaching focus and how much comfort your students need. Kibale's Makerere University station suits large mixed-ability groups, Budongo suits chimpanzee-behaviour courses that combine with Murchison Falls, and the Institute of Tropical Forest Conservation suits smaller groups focused on montane forest and gorillas.

Makerere University Biological Field Station, Kibale

The Makerere University Biological Field Station has supported research in Kibale since 1970 and expanded sharply in the early 1990s. It sits about 15 km from Fort Portal, at the foot of the Rwenzori Mountains, and can house and feed field courses of up to 60 students. There is a lecture hall, library, cafeteria and meeting room, plus more than 150 km of maintained trails through old-growth forest, swamp and regenerating land. Long-term monitoring data going back decades gives student projects something to compare against.

Budongo Conservation Field Station, near Masindi

Budongo Conservation Field Station began in 1990 as the Budongo Forest Project, founded by the anthropologist Vernon Reynolds, and took its current name in 2007. Its chimpanzees have been followed continuously since the early 1990s, which makes it a strong choice for behaviour-heavy primate field course modules. Students on a Budongo primate field course usually sleep in simple bandas rather than lodges, and the station sits on the road towards Murchison Falls, so a Nile cruise and game drive fit neatly before or after the forest weeks.

Institute of Tropical Forest Conservation, Bwindi

The Institute of Tropical Forest Conservation was set up in 1991 at Ruhija on the eastern edge of Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, and is a field station of Mbarara University of Science and Technology. You can read more on the institute's official site. Ruhija sits at around 2,350 m, so it is cooler and steeper than Kibale. It suits smaller, fitter groups interested in montane forest ecology and gorilla conservation, and it pairs naturally with a gorilla trek in the Ruhija sector.

StationBest forGroup fitPairs well with

Budongo station, near MasindiChimpanzee behaviour, long-term community dataSmall to mid-sized groups, simple bandasMurchison Falls, Ziwa Rhino Sanctuary
ITFC, Ruhija (Bwindi)Montane forest, gorilla conservationSmaller, fitter groups; high altitudeGorilla trekking, Lake Bunyonyi

Stations set their own course fees and booking rules, and they fill early for the northern summer. Contact the station first to agree dates and teaching space for your primate field course, then build transport and extensions around the confirmed block.

Permits, Research Clearance and Fees for a Primate Field Course

A teaching-only primate field course needs park entry, any activity permits such as chimpanzee tracking, and the station's own fees. If students collect data for dissertations or publication, Uganda also expects research clearance, which the host station normally helps you arrange through its university affiliation.

The Uganda National Council for Science and Technology runs the national research clearance process, and work inside a national park also needs permission from the Uganda Wildlife Authority. Start this at least three to four months before travel, and ask your station which approvals a course of your design actually needs, because a short teaching course and a multi-month research project are treated differently.

Fees for a primate field course come from the Uganda Wildlife Authority conservation tariff. The current tariff has two details course leaders often miss: foreign students on short field courses with valid student ID pay half the normal park entry for up to ten days, and Kibale gives a 20% entrance discount to groups of more than 20 on the same day.

All figures are from the UWA conservation tariff (checked November 2026) and can change without notice, so confirm them before you set student fees. Station charges for beds, meals, lecture space and research assistants on a primate field course are separate and quoted by each station. For a deeper look at the two chimpanzee permit types, see our guide to chimpanzee trekking in Kibale.

How Should You Structure a Two-Week Course?

A two-week primate field course works best as one long block at a single station, bookended by a travel day in and a short extension out. Moving bases mid-course costs teaching time, while a fixed base lets students repeat transects and build a data set worth analysing.

A sample primate field course outline from Kibale

This is one way to shape a 14-day primate field course with a Kibale base and a short Queen Elizabeth finish. A longer primate field course simply extends the project phase.

Groups who want gorillas add two nights in Bwindi after Queen Elizabeth. The road from Entebbe to Bwindi takes around 8 to 10 hours, so it only makes sense as part of a loop, and our Bwindi gorilla trekking guide explains the sectors and fitness level. Group Logistics: Vehicles, Rooming, Safety and Pricing

Group logistics for a primate field course come down to four things: enough vehicle seats with room for kit, rooming that matches the station's layout, a clear safety and medical plan, and a group price that is easy for students to pay. Getting these right early saves most of the stress on the ground.

Vehicles and transfers

We move primate field course groups in 4x4 safari vehicles with experienced driver guides, which handle the murram roads around the forest edges and give every student a window. Field kit such as GPS units and binoculars takes more space than expected, so plan spare seats. Once at the station, vehicles stay on call for town runs, clinic trips and the move to the extension.

Rooming and meals

Station rooming on a primate field course is usually shared, from dormitory-style rooms to simple bandas, with shared bathrooms. Tell students this clearly before they sign up. For the extension we switch to lodges with twin rooms, which helps morale after two weeks of early starts. Stations cater on site, so share dietary needs with the station and with us at the same time.

Safety and health

Every group should have a named first-aider, a written evacuation plan and travel insurance that covers fieldwork. We share a full plan and risk overview with leaders before travel, and recommend Flying Doctors evacuation cover for remote forest stations. Students on a primate field course must also follow distance and illness rules around apes: anyone with a cold stays out of the forest that day, because chimpanzees and gorillas catch human respiratory infections.

Group pricing logic

We quote every group personally, because the total depends on dates, numbers, rooms and permits. On our group trips, for every six paying travellers the seventh place is free, which most universities use for staff. A deposit of 30 to 40% holds the booking, and the balance is due two to four weeks before travel. Each student can pay separately, and staff can arrive on different flights. The step-by-step guide to organising a group safari explains the process in full.

A private group trip also beats joining scheduled tours with strangers: the pace follows your teaching plan, and the schedule can change if a project needs another morning in the forest.

When Is the Best Time to Run It?

The best time to run a primate field course in Uganda is June to August or December to February, Uganda's two drier spells. Forest trails are firmer, fewer days are lost to heavy rain, and June to August lines up neatly with the northern university summer break.

Primates are in the forest all year, so a wet-season primate field course still works if the timetable allows for afternoon storms. March to May and roughly October to November bring the heaviest rain; trails get muddy and some project days slip. On the plus side, the forest is green and busy, and Kibale chimpanzee tracking has a lower season rate in some wet months. Southern hemisphere universities often find December to February fits their own long break and the dry weather at the same time.

Whatever the month, plan for heat on the savannah extension and cool, damp mornings at Ruhija. Light rain gear, quick-dry clothing and gaiters suit every season; our gorilla trekking packing list works well as a base for forest kit.

Insider Tips

  • Book the station first: Teaching space for a June to August primate field course goes early; confirm it before flights or permits
  • Collect passport details early: Chimpanzee and gorilla permits are issued in each student's name
  • Carry student ID: The 50% park-entry discount for short field courses needs valid ID at the gate
  • Count the 20: Kibale's group discount applies to more than 20 people entering on the same day
  • Start clearance early: Allow three to four months if students will collect research data
  • Budget for 2027: Kibale chimpanzee permit prices are announced to rise from January 2027

Frequently Asked Questions

How long should a primate field course in Uganda be?

A primate field course in Uganda usually runs two to four weeks at one field station, plus three to five days for travel and an extension. Two weeks is enough to teach methods and run short projects. Four weeks allows proper data sets and written papers, so longer tropical biology courses at Kibale often last a month.

Do students need a research permit for a field course in Uganda?

Students on a teaching-only field course normally need park entry and activity permits rather than full research clearance. If they collect data for dissertations or publication, Uganda expects clearance through the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology and permission from the Uganda Wildlife Authority. Ask your host station early, as it usually guides the process.

Is there a student discount on Uganda park fees?

Uganda park fees do include a student concession: foreign students on short field courses with valid student ID pay 50% of normal park entry for up to ten days, under the Uganda Wildlife Authority tariff (checked November 2026). Kibale also gives a 20% entrance discount to groups of more than 20 on the same day. Primate permits are charged at the full rate.

Which is better for a primate course, Kibale or Budongo?

Kibale is usually better for a broad primate course with a large group, because the Makerere station houses up to 60 students and the forest holds 13 primate species. Budongo is better for smaller groups focused on chimpanzee behaviour, with a long-studied chimpanzee population and an easy link to Murchison Falls. Some universities use both in one trip.

How many students can join one course?

Most primate field courses in Uganda run with 12 to 30 students and two to four staff. The Kibale station can house and feed up to 60, while Budongo and Ruhija suit smaller groups. Forest work splits students into small teams, and gorilla treks take a maximum of eight visitors per gorilla family, so larger groups trek across several families.

Final Thoughts

Pick the station first and build everything else around it: Kibale for size and variety, Budongo for chimpanzee behaviour, Ruhija for montane forest and gorillas. With clearance started early and student ID in every pocket, a primate field course in Uganda gives students real data and a trip they remember.
